1240607.overview:
## Summary Axios for Node.js does not apply configured DNS lookup or proxy controls when a request uses `httpVersion: 2`. The HTTP/1 adapter path wraps and forwards `config.lookup`, builds normal request options, and applies proxy routing through `setProxy()`. The HTTP/2 path builds a session with `http2.connect()` using only `options.http2Options`, which drops the top-level `lookup`, `agent`, and proxy state. Applications are affected when they allow a user to influence request destinations, enable axios HTTP/2, and rely on axios `lookup` or proxy routing to prevent SSRF or enforce outbound network policy. ## Impact In affected server-side deployments, an attacker can cause axios to connect directly to destinations that the configured resolver or proxy would have rejected. Depending on reachable services, this can expose cloud metadata, internal service responses, or allow state-changing requests to internal systems. This is not an unconditional SSRF in every axios deployment. It requires `httpVersion: 2` and an application-level trust boundary where user-influenced URLs are constrained by `lookup` or proxy policy. ## Affected Functionality Affected: - Node.js HTTP adapter with `httpVersion: 2`. - `config.lookup` supplied as a DNS policy. - Explicit `config.proxy` and environment-derived proxy settings for HTTPS HTTP/2 requests. Not affected: - Browser adapters. - Node HTTP/1 requests, which pass `lookup` to the transport and apply proxy handling. - Applications that validate destination hosts independently before calling axios. ## Technical Details In `lib/adapters/http.js`, the adapter reads `lookup`, wraps it, stores it on the request `options`, and applies `setProxy()` before selecting a transport. For HTTP/2, `http2Transport.request()` builds an authority from `options.protocol`, `options.hostname`, and `options.port`, then calls: ```js const { http2Options, headers } = options; const session = http2Sessions.getSession(authority, http2Options); ``` `lib/helpers/Http2Sessions.js` ultimately calls `http2.connect(authority, options)` with only the `http2Options` object. The configured DNS lookup and the proxy or tunneling agent installed on the top-level request options are not forwarded into that call. Local verification on axios `1.18.1` showed `lookupCalls: 0` while an HTTP/2 request to a local h2 origin succeeded. A second local HTTPS h2 verification with an explicit rejecting HTTP proxy showed the origin received the request and the proxy observed no traffic. ## Proof of Concept of Attack Local constrained demonstration: 1. Start an HTTP/2 server on loopback. 2. Call `axios.get("http://localhost:/internal", { httpVersion: 2, lookup })` where `lookup` throws `EPOLICY`. 3. Observe that the request succeeds and the lookup counter remains `0`. For proxy routing: 1. Start an HTTPS HTTP/2 origin and a local HTTP proxy that rejects every request and CONNECT. 2. Call axios with `httpVersion: 2`, `http2Options: { rejectUnauthorized: false }`, and explicit `proxy`. 3. Observe that the origin receives the request and the proxy receives nothing. Expected safe behavior is that either the lookup policy blocks the request or the proxy observes and rejects the request. ## Workarounds Use the HTTP/1 adapter path for requests that depend on axios `lookup` or proxy controls. Alternatively, enforce destination allow/deny policy before calling axios, outside the adapter transport path.

Original report

 ### Summary I found that Axios does not apply the configured `lookup` function or proxy when a request uses `httpVersion: 2`. The HTTP/1 adapter applies both controls, but the HTTP/2 path connects straight to the URL's hostname using `http2.connect()`. This matters for server applications that accept a user-influenced URL and use a custom DNS lookup or mandatory outbound proxy to prevent SSRF. Switching the Axios instance to HTTP/2 silently removes those controls, allowing the request to reach an address the application intended to block. I reproduced this on the current npm release, Axios 1.18.1. ### Details The HTTP adapter reads and wraps the caller's `lookup` function, builds the normal request options, and calls `setProxy()`: - `lib/adapters/http.js`, around lines 530-578: reads and wraps `lookup` - `lib/adapters/http.js`, around lines 895-954: adds `lookup` to `options` and applies `setProxy()` For HTTP/2, however, the adapter selects `http2Transport`. That transport creates an authority from the destination and only passes `options.http2Options` to the session pool: ```js const { http2Options, headers } = options; const session = http2Sessions.getSession(authority, http2Options); ``` `lib/helpers/Http2Sessions.js` then calls: ```js const session = http2.connect(authority, options); ``` At this point `options` is only the `http2Options` object. The top-level `lookup`, the proxy tunnelling agent created by `setProxy()`, and the selected `httpAgent`/`httpsAgent` are not forwarded. The request therefore uses the system resolver and opens a direct connection to the origin. The same root cause affects both explicit proxy configuration and environment-derived proxy configuration. I kept the PoC local and used an explicit proxy so the result does not depend on shell environment variables. ### PoC I attached [axios_http2_transport_controls_poc.mjs](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lKXBOLDoysOFRmaRyV1tMVLx3P0Ah4gV/view?usp=sharing). The PoC is entirely local and sets up three pieces: 1. An HTTPS origin with HTTP/2 enabled. If reached, it records the request and returns `REACHED_BLOCKED_ORIGIN`. 2. An HTTP proxy that records traffic but rejects every normal request and every CONNECT request with `502 Bad Gateway`. 3. A custom Axios `lookup` callback that rejects every DNS lookup with an `EPOLICY` error. The first request is an HTTP/1 control request. It uses the blocking `lookup` callback and has proxying disabled. Axios calls the callback, receives `EPOLICY`, and does not reach the origin. This confirms that the callback works and that the hostname is blocked through the normal adapter path. The second request targets the same URL with `httpVersion: 2`. It is given both security controls: the same blocking `lookup` callback and the rejecting proxy. If Axios honors either one, this request cannot reach the origin. It should fail with `EPOLICY`, or it should reach the proxy and receive its `502` response. Instead, the request returns HTTP 200 with `REACHED_BLOCKED_ORIGIN`. The lookup counter does not increase, and the proxy records no request or CONNECT attempt. The origin is the only server that records traffic. This shows that the HTTP/2 path skipped both controls and connected directly using the system resolver. To reproduce, run the attachment from the root of an Axios checkout: Run it from the root of an Axios checkout: ```bash git checkout v1.18.1 npm install --ignore-scripts node /path/to/axios_http2_transport_controls_poc.mjs ``` Relevant output from my run: ```json { "axiosVersion": "1.18.1", "configuredControls": { "lookup": "reject every DNS lookup with EPOLICY", "proxy": "http://127.0.0.1: (reject every request)" }, "http1Control": "EPOLICY: blocked by application DNS policy", "http2Result": { "status": 200, "data": "REACHED_BLOCKED_ORIGIN" }, "lookupCalls": 1, "proxyObservedTraffic": false, "events": [ { "server": "origin", "protocol": "h2", "path": "/internal" } ] } ``` The important parts of the output are: - `http1Control` contains `EPOLICY`, proving the DNS policy blocks the destination under HTTP/1. - `lookupCalls` is still `1` after both requests, proving HTTP/2 never called the configured resolver. - `proxyObservedTraffic` is `false`, proving HTTP/2 did not use the configured proxy. - `http2Result.status` is `200`, and the sole event belongs to the origin, proving Axios connected directly to the blocked destination. ### Impact The vulnerable configuration is a Node.js application that: - enables Axios HTTP/2 using `httpVersion: 2`; - lets an application user influence the request destination; and - relies on Axios's `lookup` option or proxy routing to enforce a destination or egress policy. In that setup, an unauthenticated application user may be able to make the server connect directly to loopback, private-network, or link-local services that the lookup policy or proxy would have rejected. Depending on the reachable service, this can expose cloud credentials or internal data, modify internal services, or affect availability. HTTP/2 support is marked experimental, but neither the HTTP/2 documentation nor the proxy documentation says that `lookup` and proxy controls are ignored. The proxy documentation states that HTTPS requests are sent through a CONNECT tunnel. More importantly, Axios's threat model tells callers that destination validation is their responsibility; this behavior silently bypasses such caller-supplied validation. I did not test against any third-party or production service. The PoC only uses listeners on my own machine.
---

### Impact
When server credentials are created with the `requireClientCertificate` option set to `false`, `getAuthContext` does not distinguish between authorized and unauthorized certificates in its return value. This can create improper authentication vulnerabilities for `@grpc/grpc-js` users who use the result of `getAuthContext` for authentication.

In particular, `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` can both set the `requireClientCertificate` option to `false` and use the return value of `getAuthContext` for RBAC authentication in some configurations.

### Patches

This vulenrability is fixed in 1.13.6 and 1.14.5.

### Workarounds
`@grpc/grpc-js` users using `getAuthContext` this way can avoid this problem by setting `requireClientCertificate` to `true`. `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` users using RBAC can avoid this by setting the `require_client_certificate` field to `true` in the DownstreamTlsContext in the xDS configuration.

1240624.overview:
### Impact
If an application method handler crashes, the error message is included in the status message sent to the client. This can leak to the client any sensitive data that may be included in the error message. This impacts anyone using `@grpc/grpc-js` to run servers.

### Patches
This vulnerability is fixed in 1.13.6 and 1.14.5.

### Workarounds
This can be avoided by using a top-level error handler in method handlers to strip out sensitive error information.

1241210.overview:
### Impact

`proxy-addr` determines which network hops are trusted proxies so that `X-Forwarded-For` can be believed. When an application configures a trust subnet as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address with a short prefix, such as `::ffff:10.0.0.0/8` (the correct spelling is `::ffff:10.0.0.0/104`), the subnet compiles with all-zero leading bits and matches every IPv4 address instead of the block it names. The same happens for any IPv6 trust subnet with zero leading bits, such as `::/1`.

Every unauthenticated client is then trusted as a proxy at hop 0, so `proxyaddr(req, trust)`, and therefore `req.ip` and `req.ips` in Express, returns whatever the client sends in `X-Forwarded-For`. This defeats IP-based access control, rate limiting, geolocation, and audit logging. The misconfiguration compiles without any error, and the same block written correctly behaves correctly, so the difference is not visible from the configuration.

### Patches

Upgrade to `proxy-addr` 2.0.8. An IPv4 address now matches an IPv6 trust subnet only when that subnet is a genuine IPv4-mapped subnet whose prefix covers the mapped marker.

### Workarounds

Write IPv4 trust subnets in plain IPv4 notation (for example `10.0.0.0/8`). If IPv4-mapped IPv6 notation is required, use the full form so the prefix covers the mapped marker (for example `::ffff:10.0.0.0/104` for the `10.0.0.0/8` block).

1241221.overview:
### Impact

A vulnerability in compression `< 1.8.2` allows an attacker to trigger a Denial of Service (DoS) by disconnecting while a compressed response is being sent. When the client aborts the connection before the response finishes, the zlib stream created to compress that response is never destroyed, so each aborted compressed response leaks its native zlib memory. Repeated aborted requests can exhaust available memory. All applications using compression are affected.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to `1.8.2`.

### Workarounds

None.

1241676.overview:
## Summary

`Handlebars.precompile()` generates JavaScript source that is commonly embedded in browser `<script>` elements. Before the fix, static template text containing `</script>` was emitted unchanged. HTML parsers recognize `</script>` even inside a JavaScript string literal, closing the surrounding script element and allowing following attacker-controlled markup to be parsed and executed.

This affects applications that precompile attacker-controlled templates and embed the generated source directly in an HTML `<script>` element. It does not affect ordinary server-side rendering or precompiled templates delivered as external JavaScript files.

## Details

Static text is serialized by `quotedString()` in `lib/handlebars/compiler/code-gen.js`. The generated JavaScript is valid, but JavaScript quoting alone does not make it safe to embed in HTML. In HTML script data, the sequence `</script>` terminates the element regardless of JavaScript string context.

On affected releases, this template:

```handlebars
safe</script><script>alert("XSS")</script><script>
```

could produce generated source containing:

```js
return 'safe</script><script>alert("XSS")</script><script>';
```

When included inline in an HTML document, the first `</script>` closes the script containing the precompiled template. The next `<script>` element is then parsed as HTML and executes.

## Proof of Concept

```js
const Handlebars = require('handlebars');

const template = 'safe</script><script>alert("XSS")</script><script>';
const output = Handlebars.precompile(template);

console.log(output.includes('</script>'));
```

Affected versions print `true`. Embedding `output` directly in an inline `<script>` element allows the injected script tag to be parsed by the browser.

## Workarounds

- Do not inline precompiled output from untrusted templates into HTML documents.
- Serve generated precompiled templates as external JavaScript files where practical.

## Credits

Reported by Curly-Haired-Baboon Aka Laplas

1241677.overview:
## Summary

`Handlebars.compile()` and `Handlebars.precompile()` accept a pre-parsed AST as well as a template string. Handlebars 4.7.9 added validation for such ASTs. It only checks values on `PathExpression`, `NumberLiteral` and `BooleanLiteral` nodes, and the compiler still writes several other AST values into the generated JavaScript unchecked.

If an application passes an untrusted object to `compile()` or `precompile()`, such as a parsed JSON request body, that object can carry arbitrary JavaScript. With `compile()`, the code runs on the server when the template renders. With `precompile()`, it ends up in the precompiled output and runs wherever that output is loaded.

Applications that only ever pass template **strings** are not affected.

This bypasses the AST validation added in 4.7.9 for GHSA-2w6w-674q-4c4q, GHSA-xhpv-hc6g-r9c6 and GHSA-3mfm-83xf-c92r.

## Details

The 4.7.9 validator runs in `parseWithoutProcessing()` and walks the whole AST. It only checks values on nodes whose `type` is `PathExpression`, `NumberLiteral` or `BooleanLiteral`. It passes over plain objects without a `type`, and over strings and other non-object values. The compiler reads these values from other places and writes them into the generated code as-is:

| AST value | Written into generated code as | Compile options needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Program.blockParams.length` | `container.program(<index>, data, <length>)` | none (default options) |
| `depth` on a param that is not a `PathExpression`, e.g. a `StringLiteral` | `depths[<depth>]` | `stringParams: true` |
| A `StringLiteral.value` that is not a string | raw JavaScript literal | `stringParams: true` |
| A `PathExpression.original` that is not a string | raw JavaScript literal | `stringParams: true` |

The first row works with default options. A `Program` with `blockParams: { "length": "<JS expression>" }` passes validation because:

1. the `blockParams` object has no `type`, so none of the type-specific checks apply, and
2. the walker skips the string under `length` because it is not an object.

The compiler then reads `program.blockParams.length` and writes the string directly into the template function. The `container.program(...)` call is part of the helper options object, which is built before the helper is looked up. The code therefore runs on render even if the block's helper does not exist.

## Proof of Concept

1. Start a server that compiles request input:

```js
import express from "express";
import Handlebars from "handlebars";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.post("/api/render", (req, res) => {
  const template = Handlebars.compile(req.body.text); // `text` may be an object, not a string
  res.send(template());
});

app.listen(2123);
```

2. Save this request body as `poc.json`. `missingHelper` does not need to exist:

```json
{
  "text": {
    "type": "Program",
    "loc": { "start": { "line": 1, "column": 0 } },
    "body": [
      {
        "type": "BlockStatement",
        "path": {
          "type": "PathExpression", "data": false, "depth": 0,
          "parts": ["missingHelper"], "original": "missingHelper",
          "loc": { "start": { "line": 1, "column": 0 } }
        },
        "params": [],
        "program": {
          "type": "Program",
          "blockParams": {
            "length": "(()=>{throw new Error('Injected code ran as uid ' + process.getuid())})()"
          },
          "body": [],
          "loc": { "start": { "line": 1, "column": 0 } }
        },
        "openStrip": { "open": false, "close": false },
        "inverseStrip": { "open": false, "close": false },
        "closeStrip": { "open": false, "close": false },
        "loc": { "start": { "line": 1, "column": 0 } }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

3. Send the request:

```sh
curl -s -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:2123/api/render' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @poc.json
```

The server responds with HTTP 500 and an error page showing the injected code ran inside the Node.js process:

```
Error: Injected code ran as uid 1000
```

## Impact

An application is affected if untrusted input can reach `Handlebars.compile()` or `Handlebars.precompile()` as an object instead of a string. A common way this happens is passing a field from a JSON request body straight to `compile()`.

- **`compile()`**: arbitrary JavaScript runs in the Node.js process with the application's privileges (remote code execution).
- **`precompile()`**: the injected code is written into the precompiled template and runs wherever that template is loaded, for example in users' browsers.


## Workarounds

- **Validate input type** before calling `Handlebars.compile()`: ensure the argument is always a  `string`, never a plain object or JSON-deserialized value.
  ```javascript
  if (typeof templateInput !== 'string') {
    throw new TypeError('Template must be a string');
  }
  ```
- Use the Handlebars **runtime-only** build (`handlebars/runtime`) on the server if templates are  pre-compiled at build time; `compile()` will be unavailable.

1243066.overview: Zod schema-validation library through 4.6.5 contains an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability that allows attackers to exhaust memory by submitting a large array to an application using an array schema without a length constraint. Attackers can exploit the handleArrayResult parse logic in $ZodArray, which accumulates every validation issue for each failing element with no cap or early termination, causing the process to allocate excessive issue objects and crash due to out-of-memory conditions.

1243073.overview:
### Impact

A single request can crash any application using `body-parser` with default options. When a request carries a `Content-Encoding` (for example `gzip`), `body-parser` pipes it into a decompression stream and, after reading the body, leaves that stream piped with no error listener. A payload of one valid compressed frame followed by trailing bytes decodes and the application responds normally, but the trailing bytes then reach the already-finished decoder, which emits an error that is re-thrown as an uncaught exception and terminates the process. No authentication or matching route is required, since parsing runs before routing.

### Patches

Fixed in body-parser 2.4.0 and 1.20.9. Upgrade to one of these versions.

### Workarounds

Pass `inflate: false` to the body-parser middleware if the application does not need to accept compressed request bodies. This rejects encoded requests before any decompression stream is created.
1243073.title: body-parser vulnerable to Denial of Service via trailing bytes after a compressed request body

1243079.overview:
### Impact

undici's `EventSource` client can be driven to exhaust process memory by a malicious or compromised Server-Sent Events peer. By sending millions of tiny completed `data:` fields with no blank event separator, or a single unfinished line split across many chunks, the parser retains a growing amount of per-field and per-chunk state. The byte-based `maxEventSize` and `maxResponseSize` limits do not bound that retained state, and `maxResponseSize` is enforced on the compressed body before decompression, so a small compressed response can expand into enough retained memory to terminate the process. The application only needs to maintain an `EventSource` connection to an untrusted peer, which controls only the response. Availability is the only impact.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`, which bound the retained EventSource parser state (the number of `data` fields and buffered chunks, the unfinished-line length, and per-field byte totals) independently of the byte limits.

### Workarounds

None.
1243079.title: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unbounded memory in the EventSource parser

1243114.overview:
### Impact

undici's `fetch()` crashes the Node.js process when a malicious server returns a response with more than five content codings and closes the connection before sending the body. undici rejects such responses (a content-encoding limit), but it created the internal response stream before that check and returned without attaching an error listener or aborting the request. The early close then surfaces a content-length mismatch on that orphaned internal stream, which Node.js treats as an unhandled `error` and terminates the process. A remote, unauthenticated server can trigger this with a single response, even when the application correctly catches the `fetch()` rejection. undici 6.x, 7.x, and 8.x are affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`. undici now validates the content-encoding chain before creating the internal body stream and aborts the response when the limit is exceeded, so no error can surface on an orphaned stream.

### Workarounds

None.
1243114.title: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unhandled error on excessive content-encodings

1243476.overview:
### Impact

undici's `Agent` passes its constructor options through a JSON-based deep clone (`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))`) before forwarding them to each per-origin `Pool`. JSON cannot represent functions, so a caller-supplied `tls` option containing a `checkServerIdentity` callback is silently dropped before it reaches the TLS layer. As a result, a TLS peer whose certificate a custom `checkServerIdentity` was written to reject, but which passes Node's default hostname and chain checks, is silently accepted when the request is made through `Agent`. Because `Agent` is the default dispatcher behind `request`, `fetch`, and `setGlobalDispatcher`, this is the path most applications use. `EnvHttpProxyAgent` is also affected on its direct and `NO_PROXY` routes, which delegate to an internal `Agent`.

Only applications that pass a function-valued `tls` option (such as a custom `checkServerIdentity` for certificate or public-key pinning) are affected. Passing the same options through `connect` is not affected. This is the `Agent` counterpart of the `BalancedPool` certificate validation bypass fixed in CVE-2026-84961.

### Patches

Upgrade to undici `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`. `Agent` now preserves the `tls` option outside the JSON clone, so custom TLS verification callbacks are forwarded to each origin unchanged.

### Workarounds

Pass the TLS options through `connect` instead of `tls`. For proxied `EnvHttpProxyAgent` destinations, use `requestTls` / `proxyTls`.
1243476.title: undici vulnerable to TLS certificate validation bypass via dropped tls options in Agent

1243479.overview:
## Impact

undici crashes the client process when a TLS 1.2 server renegotiates after the connection is established and presents a different, CA-trusted certificate whose hostname does not match the requested host. Node.js re-runs hostname verification on the renegotiated handshake and destroys the socket with `ERR_TLS_CERT_ALTNAME_INVALID`. undici's established socket error handler asserted that this error code could never occur, so the peer-controlled error became an uncaught `AssertionError` that terminates the Node.js process. Both the HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 paths are affected.

A malicious or compromised HTTPS endpoint reached through undici or the global `fetch()` can crash the client with a single server-initiated renegotiation, taking down all in-flight requests and background work in the process. Only TLS 1.2 is affected, because TLS 1.3 does not support renegotiation. Exploitation does not require a CA compromise: the attacker controls the endpoint and can present two ordinary valid certificates, the first matching the requested URL and the second intentionally not matching it.

## Patches

Upgrade to undici 6.29.1, 7.30.1, or 8.12.2.

## Workarounds

Restrict outbound connections to TLS 1.3, for example by setting `connect: { minVersion: 'TLSv1.3', maxVersion: 'TLSv1.3' }` on the client or agent, so that renegotiation cannot occur, when the target endpoints support TLS 1.3.
1243479.title: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via TLS 1.2 certificate-changing renegotiation

1243482.overview:
### Impact

undici's WebSocket client (including Node.js's bundled `globalThis.WebSocket`) can be driven to exhaust process memory by a malicious or compromised WebSocket server. For every PING frame received, the receiver automatically writes a PONG response to the socket and ignores the `false` return value from `socket.write()`, which is a backpressure signal, so a server that streams small PING frames while never reading the client's PONGs makes the outbound write queue and heap grow without bound until the Node.js process runs out of memory and terminates. The attack is remote and unauthenticated, needs only a normal WebSocket connection, and is asymmetric: small inbound PINGs produce a much larger retained outbound queue. Availability is the only impact. undici 5.x, 6.x, 7.x, and 8.x are affected; the WebSocket client was introduced in 5.15.0.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`, which pause WebSocket frame parsing when the automatic PONG response hits socket backpressure and resume on drain, bounding the outbound queue.

### Workarounds

None.
1243482.title: undici WebSocket client vulnerable to Denial of Service via unbounded automatic PONG buffering

1243505.overview: deepmerge through 4.3.1 contains a prototype poisoning vulnerability in the mergeObject() function that fails to properly validate keys being written to target objects. Attackers can supply malicious source objects in merge operations to inject attacker-controlled properties into the returned object's prototype, causing applications to inherit unintended values when accessing properties without own-property checks.
1243505.title: deepmerge mergeObject() allows prototype poisoning of returned objects

1243687.overview:
## Summary

`qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })` throws an uncaught `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` when an array in `obj` contains an element that carries an own, non-callable `toString` property (for example `{ a: [ { toString: 'x' } ] }`). A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can influence an object that the application later re-serializes with the comma array format triggers the throw. In a service that lacks a synchronous error boundary around the serialization call, the uncaught exception crashes the worker process, producing a denial of service.

## Root Cause

When `arrayFormat: 'comma'` is selected, the comma branch collapses the whole array into a single value via `Array.prototype.join`, or, under `encodeValuesOnly: true`, maps each element through the value encoder before joining. Both paths perform an implicit string coercion (`ToPrimitive` with hint `"string"`) on each element. For an object whose own `toString` is a non-callable value, coercion skips the shadowed non-callable `toString`, falls through to `Object.prototype.valueOf` (which returns the object rather than a primitive), and throws. The comma branch runs this coercion before the per-element null and skip handling in the main loop, so nothing downstream can neutralize the hostile element, and the throw is never caught inside the library.

```text
lib/stringify.js  (comma-array branch)
  line 152-154: obj = utils.maybeMap(obj, function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); });  // encodeValuesOnly path
  line 156:     objKeys = [{ value: obj.length > 0 ? obj.join(',') || null : void undefined }];   // default comma path
lib/utils.js
  line 292:     string = String(str);   // value encoder coercion reached via the encodeValuesOnly path
```

## Impact

Prerequisites: the application calls `qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` (a documented, supported option) on an object whose shape can be influenced by attacker input. Attacker-controllable sources include `qs.parse(input, { allowPrototypes: true })`, which retains a `toString` segment (Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's `extended` query parser, and body-parser's `extended` urlencoded parser all set it), `qs.parse(input, { plainObjects: true })`, whose null-prototype elements throw even without a `toString` key (eg, `a[][b]=c`), and `JSON.parse` of a request body, which needs no qs parse option at all. No authentication or user interaction is required. Demonstrated capability: a single request forces an uncaught synchronous `TypeError` in the serialization call. In a naive single-process Node service with no synchronous error boundary, this crashes the process and takes the service offline (availability impact). Under a framework such as Express that traps synchronous handler throws, the plausible outcome is a per-request 500 rather than a full outage; that lower-impact case is noted but not the worst credible supported deployment. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact, no memory unsafety, and no prototype pollution.

## Proof of Concept

`Install qs at the affected version (for example 6.16.0) and run the following script with Node.js. No network setup is required; it demonstrates the throw in isolation.`

```js
var qs = require('qs');

// Source A: qs.parse with allowPrototypes retains the hostile toString segment
qs.stringify(qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x', { allowPrototypes: true }), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Source B: a JSON request body, no qs parse option needed
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Also affected: the encodeValuesOnly sub-path
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma', encodeValuesOnly: true });
```

```text
A default-join (allowPrototypes) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
B default-join (JSON.parse) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
C encodeValuesOnly path => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
N2 callable toString => NO THROW; output="a=z"
N3 isBuffer vector (CVE-2026-82417) => NO THROW; output="a%5Bconstructor%5D%5BisBuffer%5D=x"
qs version: 6.16.0
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** A remote, unauthenticated request reaches an endpoint whose handler eventually serializes attacker-influenced data with `qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })`.
2. **Control:** The attacker supplies data that becomes `{ a: [ { toString: <non-callable value> } ] }`, either via `a[0][toString]=x` parsed with `allowPrototypes`, or via a JSON body `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}`.
3. **Path:** In `stringify`, the primitive/buffer guard at `lib/stringify.js:134` is false for an array, so control reaches the comma branch at `lib/stringify.js:149`.
4. **Guard:** On the `encodeValuesOnly` path, the closure `v == null ? v : encoder(v)` at `lib/stringify.js:152-154` passes only `null`/`undefined` through; a non-null object still reaches the encoder. The default path skips that closure entirely and reaches `obj.join(',')` at `lib/stringify.js:156` with no guard at all.
5. **Primitive:** The element is coerced to a string (`Array.prototype.join`, or `String(str)` at `lib/utils.js:292`). `ToPrimitive` skips the non-callable own `toString`, `valueOf` returns the object, and a `TypeError` is thrown.
6. **Result:** The uncaught synchronous exception propagates out of the serialization call, failing the request and, in a service without a synchronous error boundary, crashing the process (denial of service).

## Bypass Evidence

This is a different element type on the code path CVE-2026-8723 (GHSA-q8mj-m7cp-5q26) patched, plus the default comma path, which that fix never covered. CVE-2026-8723 addressed a `TypeError` crash on `null`/`undefined` entries in the comma plus `encodeValuesOnly` path. Its fix (commit 21f80b3) wraps the encoder in `function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); }`, so it only passes `null` and `undefined` through. A non-null element with a hostile own `toString` fails the `v == null` test, so the encoder still runs and still throws; the encodeValuesOnly case (case C above) throws on the exact fixed code. The default comma path (`encodeValuesOnly` unset, the library default) never entered that fix at all: `git log -S "obj.join(','" -- lib/stringify.js` shows no security fix has ever touched the `obj.join(',')` line, and cases A and B throw with `encodeValuesOnly` unset. The related isBuffer hardening for CVE-2026-82417 (commit e83d321) is a different sink at the `lib/stringify.js:134` guard, which is never entered for the array element; the negative control `{a:{constructor:{isBuffer:'x'}}}` serializes cleanly. Disproof attempts that failed: a `valueOf`-only object does not throw (it serializes to `[object Object]`), confirming the trigger is an element with no callable `toString` (an own non-callable `toString`, or a null-prototype object with no `toString` at all, as `qs.parse` produces under `plainObjects`); nested arrays (`{"a":[[{"toString":"x"}]]}`) throw the same way; a callable `toString` serializes cleanly; and the default (non-comma) array format serializes cleanly, confirming the comma format is required. All positive and negative cases were reproduced on the exact published 6.16.0 artifact.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: npm`
- `Package: qs`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 6.7.0, <= 6.16.0`
- `Latest release checked: 6.16.0 (npm latest; git tag v6.16.0)`
- `Fix status: fixed in 6.16.1 (a952e75)`

The `arrayFormat: 'comma'` join sink was introduced in qs 6.7.0, so 6.7.0 is the lower boundary; releases before 6.7.0 lack the sink. No released version fixes this vector, and the latest published release (6.16.0) reproduces the throw, so the closed upper bound `<= 6.16.0` covers every affected release. The `encodeValuesOnly` sub-path was added later, but the default comma-join vector already affects 6.7.0, so 6.7.0 governs the lower boundary.

## Suggested Fix

The comma array serialization must not allow an implicit string coercion of an array element to throw an uncaught exception. Coercion of each comma element should be performed defensively (for example by wrapping the join and per-element encode so that a coercion failure is caught and handled), and this protection must cover both the default `obj.join(',')` path and the `encodeValuesOnly` encoder path, not only the previously patched `null`/`undefined` case. As an interim mitigation without a code change, applications can avoid `arrayFormat: 'comma'` when serializing data derived from untrusted input, sanitize parsed objects (avoid `allowPrototypes`/`plainObjects` on untrusted input and strip unexpected own properties), or wrap `qs.stringify` calls in a synchronous error boundary so a coercion failure cannot crash the process.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

---

## Independent report by @Lucidsec

The following was reported separately, after this advisory, and is merged here as a duplicate.

### Summary

In project [qs](https://github.com/ljharb/qs), in versions `>= 6.7.0, <= 6.16.0` (every version that supports `arrayFormat: 'comma'`), `qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` can throw an uncaught `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` when an array element has a non-callable own `toString`. It is fixed in 6.16.1. Related: CWE-248 and CWE-704.

### Technical Details

`qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` joins an array at `lib/stringify.js:156` via `obj.join(',')`. An element whose own `toString` is not callable makes `Array.prototype.join` throw. There is no type check and no catch on that path.

A second path exists with `encodeValuesOnly`: at `lib/stringify.js:151-154`, `maybeMap` only skips `v == null`, then `lib/utils.js:292` does `String(str)` and throws the same `TypeError` (this second site exists since v6.11.1; before that, the same input throws at `join`).

Who can trigger: someone who can shape an array element passed to `stringify`. The host must use non-default `arrayFormat: 'comma'`. Default `arrayFormat` `indices` does not fold arrays and is not affected. A parse-then-stringify path also needs `plainObjects: true` (null-prototype elements from `lib/parse.js:200`) or `allowPrototypes: true` (which Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's `extended` query parser, and body-parser's `extended` urlencoded parser all set). Default `qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x')` returns `{}` because the prototype guard drops `toString`. Direct JSON handed to `stringify` can supply `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}`.

Cause: the comma fold at `lib/stringify.js:149-156` collapses the array into a single value before the main loop at `lib/stringify.js:172-212`, so `skipNulls` and `strictNullHandling` only ever see the joined value, never individual elements. `isNonNullishPrimitive` / `isBuffer` at `lib/stringify.js:134` inspect the whole value, not each element. A normal object uses `Object.prototype.toString` and becomes `[object Object]`. An own non-callable `toString` is skipped, `valueOf` returns the object, and `join` throws. (The skipped TODO test at `test/stringify.js:684-689` uses a plain `{ b: 1 }` element, which does not throw; it covers the separate question of what comma format should output for object elements, not this crash.) Earlier comma crash fixes did not cover object elements.

### Impact

One small input makes that serialization path throw a synchronous, catchable `TypeError`. Behind a framework error boundary (eg, a synchronous Express handler), the request fails with a 500 and the process survives. In a host with no error boundary (eg, a bare `http.createServer` handler), the uncaught exception exits the process (the client sees `ECONNRESET`). Availability only.

### Proof of Concept

<details>
<summary>Show the proof of concept</summary>

Checked on the latest commit that was checked: `07b1d4d82c8f9301c105ea4b94fa2302cfd6e8b4`. Still present. Demonstrated.

- Payload `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}` throws at `lib/stringify.js:156`.
- Baseline `{"a":["x","y"]}` returns 200 with body `a=x%2Cy`.
- A plain object element stringifies to `a=%5Bobject%20Object%5D` and does not throw.
- `encodeValuesOnly: true` throws via `utils.js:292`.
- `plainObjects` parse plus comma throws.

</details>

### Suggested Fix

Before `join`, map elements with the existing primitive check; skip or replace non-primitives so `join` cannot throw. On the `encodeValuesOnly` path, do not send non-primitives into `String()`. Optionally guard `lib/utils.js:292`. Add new regression tests.

1244003.overview:
### Summary

follow-redirects 1.16.0 and 1.16.1 validate the documented sensitiveHeaders option with instanceof Array. An array created in another JavaScript realm is silently replaced with an empty list, so a caller-declared custom credential header can be forwarded to an attacker-controlled cross-origin redirect destination.

### Details

Affected versions

The sensitiveHeaders option was introduced in 1.16.0. Published 1.16.0 and 1.16.1 both reproduced, giving a tested affected range of 1.16.0 through 1.16.1. The source checkout was pinned at revision 46301256333c90b7faac7aa126effe72ec16d16e; the exact npm 1.16.1 artifact reproduced independently.

Root cause

index.js resets options.sensitiveHeaders when its local isArray() helper returns false. That helper uses value instanceof Array, which depends on realm identity. The same file already uses Array.isArray(options.headers), which correctly recognizes arrays across realms.

Suggested remediation

Use Array.isArray(value) for sensitiveHeaders, then validate and normalize each member as a header-name string. Add same-realm and node:vm cross-realm tests for cross-origin redirects, including the array-form headers representation. Verify that custom sensitive names are removed while unrelated headers remain unchanged.

Duplicate review

The public advisory history contains other sensitive-header findings, including array-form headers and regular-expression handling, but focused repository searches found no report describing cross-realm validation as of 2026-10-25. A private or differently worded report may already exist.

### Proof of concept

Start two loopback HTTP servers. The first returns a 302 redirect to the second. Send X-API-Key and list that name in sensitiveHeaders, then compare a normal array with a genuine cross-realm array created by:

```js
const vm = require('node:vm');
const sensitiveHeaders = vm.runInNewContext(`['X-API-Key']`);
```

Observed against both source and the exact npm 1.16.1 package:

- Same-realm ['X-API-Key']: the redirect target did not receive the key.
- Cross-realm ['X-API-Key']: Array.isArray(value) was true, value instanceof Array was false, and the redirect target received X-API-Key.
- An unrelated X-Harmless header remained present in both cases.

The complete 3.5 KB loopback-only harness and raw JSON output are available privately.

### Impact

custom credential disclosure. Exploitation requires a direct caller or wrapper that preserves a cross-realm sensitiveHeaders array, a custom credential listed in that option, and an attacker-controlled or compromised endpoint that returns a cross-origin redirect. The directly demonstrated result is disclosure of the custom header value, potentially exposing an API key or service token until revocation.

Built-in Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, and Cookie protections remained effective. Exact Axios 1.20.0 with follow-redirects 1.16.1 did not reproduce because Axios normalized the array; this report does not claim that Axios is affected. No third-party service was tested.
1244003.title: follow-redirects: Cross-realm sensitiveHeaders arrays are discarded and custom credentials can follow redirects

1244013.overview:
### Summary

In glob 13.0.6, an aborted async walk rejects or emits an error but continues recursively reading directories in the background.

The root cause is that abort branches in src/walker.ts call cb() without returning. As a result, callers that rely on signal or AbortSignal.timeout() to bound glob traversal cost can still incur filesystem I/O and CPU work after the request has already been rejected.

### Details

This was reproduced on glob v13.0.6 (commit e80cb38ae60d6cbff9e75f39032a994858994d35).

The README documents that the signal option cancels the glob walk. However, in src/walker.ts, the following methods call cb() when this.signal?.aborted is true but do not return:

- GlobUtil.walkCB()
- GlobUtil.walkCB2()
- GlobUtil.walkCBSync()
- GlobUtil.walkCB2Sync()

Example vulnerable pattern:

if (this.signal?.aborted) cb()

Because execution continues after cb(), the walker still reaches processor.processPatterns(), readdirCB(), and recursive walkCB2() calls.

The issue was directly demonstrated against v13.0.6. A source-history review shows the same missing-return pattern is present in tagged releases from v9.0.0 through v13.0.6.

The issue affects both glob() and globStream().

Recommended fix:
Change each abort branch to return immediately:

if (this.signal?.aborted) return cb()

### Proof of concept

Environment:
- Linux x86_64
- Node.js v22.23.3
- npm 10.9.9
- glob 13.0.6

Reproduction steps:

1. Install the affected package:
   npm init -y
   npm install glob@13.0.6

2. Run the attached PoC:
   node poc/abort-continues-work.mjs

The PoC aborts after the first readdir() call, waits briefly, and counts how many more directory reads happen after the promise has already rejected.

Observed output on the vulnerable version:

{
  "rejection": "Error: probe-abort",
  "readdirCalls": 1365,
  "readdirCallsAtReject": 5,
  "readdirCallsAfterReject": 1360
}

Expected behavior:
readdirCallsAfterReject should be 0.

A second PoC using AbortSignal.timeout() also reproduces the issue:

{
  "rejection": "TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout",
  "readdirCalls": 133,
  "readdirCallsAtReject": 1,
  "readdirCallsAfterReject": 132
}

The same test against a patched build with return cb() in the four abort branches stops immediately:

{
  "readdirCalls": 1,
  "readdirCallsAtReject": 1,
  "readdirCallsAfterReject": 0
}

### Impact

This is an availability issue.

Applications that expose globbing over attacker-influenced patterns or attacker-controlled directory trees and use AbortSignal / AbortSignal.timeout() as a traversal budget can still perform significant filesystem I/O and CPU work after a request has already timed out or been canceled.

Repeated timed-out requests can stack background glob walks and degrade worker throughput or service availability.

No confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.

1244534.overview:
## Impact

The undici WebSocket client enforces `maxPayloadSize` on the cumulative byte count of fragments in a message but does not enforce a limit on the number of fragments. A malicious WebSocket server can stream many small or empty continuation frames that each pass per-frame and cumulative-size validation, collectively causing unbounded memory growth in the client process. The result is memory exhaustion and a denial of service.

Affected applications are those using the undici WebSocket client (`new WebSocket(...)`) or the `WebSocketStream` API that can be induced to connect to an attacker-controlled or compromised WebSocket endpoint.

All releases starting at undici 6.17.0 are affected.

## Patches

Upgrade to undici v6.27.0, v7.28.0 or v8.5.0.

## Workarounds

No workaround is available. The fix must be applied through an upgrade.
1244534.title: undici WebSocket client vulnerable to denial of service via fragment count bypass

1244623.overview:
minimatch 10.2.6 contains an attacker-controlled pattern amplification in firstPhasePreProcess() when optimizationLevel >= 2.

researcher: Reid Downing (b1nv0id)
files: 

- src/index.ts: 690-770
- src/index.ts: 780-796

issue:
input-controlled growth of globParts during first-phase preprocessing, followed by quadratic second-phase processing.

the **/../ transformation clones a globparts entry and appends the clone to the same globparts array:
```
parts.splice(gs, 1)
const other = parts.slice(0)
other[gs] = '**'
globParts.push(other)
```
this occurs inside a do...while (didSomething) fixpoint loop, allowing generated entries to be processed again.

the expanded globparts array is subsequently processed by secondPhasePreProcess(), which performs pairwise comparisons:
```
for (let i = 0; i < globParts.length - 1; i++) {
  for (let j = i + 1; j < globParts.length; j++) {
    this.partsMatch(...)
  }
}
```
an attacker who can supply a glob pattern can therefore cause additional pattern entries to be generated during preprocessing, followed by quadratic pairwise processing, resulting in excessive cpu and memory consumption.
1244623.title: minimatch has potential denial of service via globparts amplification

1246029.overview:
### Summary

With the non-default stopNodes option, a stop node's body with many "<a " fragments and no closing ">" anywhere after makes readStopNodeData() rescan the entire remaining input from every "<". The failed lookahead is neither cached nor bounded, so n fragments cost O(n²) before the parser throws. Availability-only (CPU exhaustion), needs the non-default stopNodes option — not benchmarked yet, see Proof of Concept.

### Details

**CWE-407** — Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity

**Code**
- `OrderedObjParser.js:520` — `parseXml()` calls `readStopNodeData()` after a matching stop node opens
- `OrderedObjParser.js:810` — calls `readTagExp()` for every non-special `<`
- `OrderedObjParser.js:688-722` — `tagExpWithClosingIndex()` scans to end-of-input and returns `undefined` when no `>` exists
- `OrderedObjParser.js:812-818` — on failure, `i` isn't advanced, so the next `<` repeats the same full scan
- `OrderedObjParser.js:423` — the main parse loop throws immediately on the same failure; only the stop-node path retries

**Root cause:** a failed closing-`>` lookahead is neither cached nor bounded — `n` copies of `<a ` with no later `>` means `n` scans over the remaining input, O(n²) work, before it finally throws.

**Fix**
1. Throw immediately in `readStopNodeData()` when `readTagExp()` returns `undefined`
2. Or break the loop on the first failed scan
3. Or find the next `>` once and reuse/bound that result
4. Add a test asserting near-linear scaling when payload size doubles

### Proof of concept

Not benchmarked — static-analysis finding, confidence 0.5.

To confirm: configure `stopNodes` matching a root element. Build input as `'<stop>' + '<a '.repeat(n)`. Time `parse()` until it throws `Unexpected end of <tag>`. Start around n=10,000 and double it — quadratic should show ~4x time per doubling, linear ~2x. Control: same input with a `>` present, or `stopNodes` unset.

### Impact

CPU-exhaustion DoS in Node.js services parsing untrusted XML with `stopNodes` enabled. A ~100KB payload is estimated at ~10⁹ character operations (roughly a second or more of blocked event loop) — analytical estimate, not a benchmark. No confidentiality/integrity impact. CVSS 3.1: `AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` (3.7, Low).
1246029.title: fast-xml-parser: Quadratic CPU consumption scanning unterminated stop-node tags

1246031.overview:
### Summary
`ed25519.verify()` does not reject public keys of small order, such as the identity point. Under such a key, a signature with `S = 0` and a small-order `R` verifies for many messages, or for every message with the identity key, without any private key. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`crypto_sign_open()` in `lib/ed25519.js` decodes the public key `A` with `unpackneg()`, which only checks that the point is on the curve, and then checks `R == [S]B - [k]A` with `k = SHA-512(R || A || M)`. Nothing rejects public keys of small order: the identity point, the other 7 points of order 2, 4 or 8, and their non-canonical encodings with `y >= p`.

With `S = 0`, the check becomes `R == [k](-A)`. For a small-order `A`, `[k](-A)` is one of at most 8 small-order points, so an attacker can make a valid signature by trying the small-order values of `R`. For the identity key (`01 00 … 00`), `R = identity` and `S = 0` verifies for every message. For the other small-order keys, a given message can be forged with high probability. No private key is involved. The `S < L` check added for CVE-2026-33895 (GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw) doesn't apply, because `S = 0` is canonical.

Keys produced by Ed25519 key generation (`ed25519.generateKeyPair()` or any RFC 8032 implementation) are never small-order, so signatures under them cannot be forged this way. Applications are affected when they verify signatures against a public key an attacker can choose (for example a key included with the signed data, a self-registered key, or a key in an attacker-controlled document) and rely on the signature being bound to the message: proof of possession, attribution, non-repudiation or deduplication.

RFC 8032 doesn't require rejecting small-order public keys, and implementations differ. libsodium rejects them, and Node.js `crypto.verify()` (OpenSSL) rejects these signatures.

The fix rejects a public key `A` when `[8]A` is the identity point. This covers all small-order points and their non-canonical encodings.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3. `ed25519.verify()` returns `false` for small-order public keys.

#### Workarounds
Before calling `ed25519.verify()` with a public key from untrusted input, reject keys whose 32-byte encoding is one of the small-order points (the identity `01 00 … 00` and the other encodings that libsodium blocks), or only verify against keys you generated or have otherwise validated.

#### Resources
- RFC 8032, Section 5.1.7 (Ed25519 verification): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032#section-5.1.7
- GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw / CVE-2026-33895 (a different Ed25519 verification issue, fixed in 1.4.0): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)
CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @analisaperlengkapan.

### Proof of concept
Identity public key `A = 01 00 … 00` (32 bytes) and signature `R = 01 00 … 00`, `S = 00 … 00` (64 bytes):

    forge.ed25519.verify({message: 'admin=true', encoding: 'utf8',
      signature: SIG, publicKey: IDENTITY});
    // <= 1.4.2: true for any message; node:crypto.verify(): false
    // 1.4.3: false

Other small-order public keys (orders 2, 4 and 8, and non-canonical encodings) give forgeries for many messages with `S = 0` and a small-order `R`.

Regression tests are in tests/unit/ed25519.js, and the reporter's PoC is in tests/pocs/ghsa-6889-vf6x-f3g5.js.

### Impact
Applications that verify Ed25519 signatures with node-forge against a public key that an attacker can choose are affected. An attacker can provide a small-order public key and then produce signatures that verify for many or all messages without a private key, defeating checks that rely on a signature being bound to its message under that key (proof of possession, attribution, non-repudiation, deduplication). Signatures under keys from honest key generation cannot be forged, and applications that only verify against their own or otherwise trusted keys are not affected.
1246031.title: Forge: Ed25519 signature verification accepts small-order public keys

1246032.overview:
### Summary
A `forge.tls` client accepts any compression method in the ServerHello, although it only offers no compression. An unknown method makes `connection.process()` throw an uncaught `Error` when the client handles ServerHelloDone, before the server is authenticated. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
The client's ClientHello offers only the `null` compression method. `tls.parseHelloMessage()` in `lib/tls.js` stores the ServerHello's `compression_method` for the client without checking it (the code has a `TODO: handle compression methods`). When the client handles ServerHelloDone it calls `tls.createConnectionState()`, which throws `Error('Unsupported compression algorithm.')` for any method other than `null` (0) and `deflate` (1). The exception propagates out of `connection.process()`.

The ServerHello isn't authenticated until the server's Finished message, so an on-path attacker can change the compression byte of a genuine ServerHello; the certificate chain still verifies. Applications that pass socket data to `process()` without catching exceptions terminate. This includes `forge.tls.wrapSocket`, which calls `process()` from its socket data handler, and `forge.http`, which uses it. A `deflate` (1) method, also never offered, makes the handshake fail later with an error instead of a crash.

Servers are not affected: a server always selects no compression.

The fix fails the handshake with an `illegal_parameter` alert, through the connection's `error` callback, when the ServerHello selects any compression method other than `null`.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Catch exceptions thrown by `connection.process()` and close the socket.

#### Resources
- RFC 5246, section 7.4.1.3 (Server Hello): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.4.1.3
- Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client crash during the handshake, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @alienkeric.

### Proof of concept
A server (or on-path attacker) sends a ServerHello with `compression_method` 0xff, followed by a valid Certificate and ServerHelloDone:

    client.handshake();
    client.process(serverHello + certificate + serverHelloDone);
    // <= 1.4.2: throws Error: Unsupported compression algorithm.
    // 1.4.3: error callback with "Unsupported compression method."

The reporter's PoC (a CA-issued server certificate and the default verify callback) is in tests/pocs/ghsa-w4xr-hqv8-ch44.js, and regression tests are in tests/unit/tls.js.

### Impact
Applications that use `forge.tls` as a client (directly, through `forge.tls.wrapSocket`, or through `forge.http`) and pass data from a network socket to `connection.process()` are affected. The server they connect to, or an on-path attacker, can make `process()` throw before the server is authenticated; if the application doesn't catch it, the Node.js process terminates, dropping all its connections. Servers built on `forge.tls` are not affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.
1246032.title: Forge: TLS client crash on an unsupported ServerHello compression method

1246033.overview:
`forge.http` trims response header and `Set-Cookie` values with the regular expression `/\s*$/`, which takes quadratic time on a long run of whitespace followed by another character. A server or on-path attacker can block a `forge.http` client for minutes with one large response header. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`_trimString()` in `lib/http.js` removes trailing whitespace with `str.replace(/\s*$/, '')`. On a string of n whitespace characters followed by a non-whitespace character, the regular expression engine tries a match at each of the n positions and scans the rest of the run each time, so the work is O(n^2). `forge.http` calls `_trimString()` on every response header value read by `response.readHeader()`, and again on cookie names and values in `response.getCookies()`. There is no limit on header size.

With Node.js 24, an 80 KB header value takes about 4 seconds to parse, and 1 MB about 10 minutes, during which the event loop (or browser tab) is blocked.

`forge.http` is not loaded by `require('node-forge')`. It is part of the `forge.all` bundle and needs a socket pool provided by the application (historically Flash sockets via `forge.xhr`), so few applications use it.

The fix trims trailing whitespace with a loop, as `lib/pem.js` has done since 1.4.1. The trimmed result is unchanged.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Limit the size of HTTP response headers before passing them to `forge.http`, for example in the socket pool's data handler.

#### Resources
- Related: GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x (ReDoS in PEM decoding, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @manus-pi.

### Proof of concept
    var response = forge.http.createResponse();
    var ws = new Array(40001).join('\t ');
    response.readHeader(forge.util.createBuffer(
      'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nX-A: a' + ws + 'X\r\n\r\n'));
    // <= 1.4.2: about 4 seconds (quadratic in the whitespace length)
    // 1.4.3: about 1 ms

Regression tests are in tests/security/ghsa-6cv4-p8m7-4r25.js.

### Impact
Applications that use `forge.http` to talk to servers they don't control are affected. The server, or an on-path attacker, can send a response header that blocks the client's event loop for minutes, denying service to everything else in the process. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.
1246033.title: Forge: ReDoS in forge.http response header and cookie trimming

1246034.overview:
### Summary
A `forge.tls` client throws an uncaught `TypeError` from `connection.process()` when it receives a ServerHello while it has no session: after a `close_notify` alert or a call to `close()`, or before `handshake()` is called. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`tls.handleHandshake()` in `lib/tls.js` updates the handshake digests with `c.session.md5.update(bytes)` before it calls the message handler. A client creates its session in `handshake()`, and `c.reset()` sets it to `null` when the connection is closed. Closing doesn't set the fail flag, and the client goes back to expecting a ServerHello, so a Handshake record received afterwards still reaches `handleHandshake()`, which throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5')`.

This happens:
- after the server sends a `close_notify` alert (at any alert level);
- after the application calls `close()`;
- before the application calls `handshake()`.

The exception propagates out of `connection.process()`. Applications that pass socket data to `process()` from a `data` event handler without catching exceptions, as in the README example, terminate. After a reset the connection uses no encryption, so an on-path attacker can inject the records even when the real server is honest.

Servers are not affected: a server creates its session when it receives a ClientHello.

The fix handles these records like other unexpected records on a closed client: they are ignored.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Catch exceptions thrown by `connection.process()` and close the socket, or stop passing socket data to `process()` once the `closed` callback has been called and until `handshake()` is called again.

#### Resources
- RFC 5246, section 7.2.1 (Closure Alerts): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.2.1
- Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client `TypeError`, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @manus-use.

### Proof of concept
    var c = forge.tls.createConnection({server: false, ...});
    c.handshake();
    // warning close_notify alert, then an empty ServerHello, in separate
    // process() calls
    c.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('15030100020100'));
    c.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('160301000402000000'));
    // <= 1.4.2: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5')
    // 1.4.3: the record is ignored

The reporter's PoC is in tests/pocs/ghsa-j8rw-jp99-435v.js, and regression tests are in tests/unit/tls.js.

### Impact
Applications that use `forge.tls` as a client and pass data from a network socket to `connection.process()` are affected. The server they connect to, or an on-path attacker, can make `process()` throw; if the application doesn't catch it, the Node.js process terminates, dropping all its connections. Servers built on `forge.tls` are not affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.
1246034.title: Forge: TLS client crash on a handshake record received without a session
